utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-R77, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin concerning allegations against Milka Maglov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Appearances. Now, Ms. Maglov, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, there is a technical hitch here. I am not receiving the transcript. On the notebook, yes, but on the other monitor, on the main monitor, I'm not receiving any transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the technician is fixing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Brenda J. Hollis, and I appearing as the amicus curiae Prosecutor in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. And that brings me to the first problem that we have. The last time we had an appearance, and that was in the Pre-Trial Conference that we had here, you had informed the Chamber, Mrs. Maglov, that it was your decision at the time to defend yourself. Is that the situation today? Is that still the situation today?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I have to apologise if I have disrupted the proceedings in any way. However, I did not expect to receive the Prosecution motion to amend the indictment, and I expected to receive the entire correspondence in a language that I understand. Since that time, the situation has become more complicated because I have to inform the Chamber, unfortunately, that I still do not have the pre-trial brief in B/C/S. I still do not have, apart from your decision and the witness statements disclosed by the Prosecution, and the motion to amend the indictment, apart from these documents, I have not received anything else in a language I understand. In this situation, it is very difficult for me to communicate with the Registry, and for all these reasons, I have come to realise that in legal matters I'm not in possession of a sufficient number of elements. In the situation I find myself in, being dislocated from this place, and for all these reasons, I have decided to ask for legal assistance. That is, for counsel. I asked the Registry originally to appoint my daughter, Marela Jevtovic, as my assistant, and they replied that they could not approve a member of my family, although I did not ask for her to be paid. I asked for her to appear pro bono. I received the response only on Friday evening, I think, telling me that I can engage her if I wish to do so, this however, is still a problem because three or four days before I set out on my trip to The Hague, I couldn't do anything else but keep telephoning the Registry, the embassy, to see whether I would get approval, only to receive approval finally on Thursday the 11th -- I apologise, the 12th, at 1300 hours when I received a letter from the Registry informing me that approval would be granted for a visa and that I was to appear at the embassy. I was to come to the embassy. It takes me eight hours to reach Belgrade from Banja Luka. So I was unable to make it during working hours on the same day. I set out as soon as I could. I went to the embassy on Friday during the normal office hours, and we were informed that we would be invited to come back when approval was granted. This did not happen on the same day, however. So we again contacted the Registry, and they informed us again that we should wait to be called to the embassy. And this was not the first time that such a thing had happened. The same thing happened on the previous occasion. The embassy official had to come to the embassy outside working hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you, because I would like to restrict the debate at the moment or the discussion at the moment only on whether you still stand by your decision to defend yourself or whether you would -- whether you are seeking for legal aid from this Tribunal. So my first question is are you seeking for legal aid from this Tribunal? And I would like a straightforward yes or no answer. Do you want this Tribunal to appoint you a lawyer to defend you and pay the expenses? Or that lawyer? That's my first question. And please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So at this point, I think the rest of the discussion has to be for the time being suspended. I have two officers from the office waiting outside. The idea is to get information, because I had information that you had made such a request last week, and I want to make sure that you had done so and what the position is. So could you please escort the two officers from OLAD's office. And we clear this up first. The important thing is that exactly they have a microphone available. MR. VAN de VLIET: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I have your names. Could you identify yourselves, please. MR. VAN de VLIET: Yes, my name is Bas Van de Vliet, I am the acting chief of the Office of Legal Aid and Detention Matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And madame.

utterances.speaker: MS. VICENTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Alejandra Vicente for the Office of Legal Aid and Detention Matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I have been informed of two things by Ms. Maglov. The first is that she is here and now requesting legal aid, and I would ask you then to brief us on this, what the procedure is, because I know that this cannot be dealt with here and now as procedure to be followed. And the second thing is that I understand or I have been given reason to understand that an ad hoc request was made sometime last week to the Office of the Registrar. How was it made, Mrs. Maglov? By means of a letter, by means of email? How was it made?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By email. I sent the standard form by email, but what I wish to say now is that if an appointment were made now, that would require a postponement of these proceedings. I wish to say that I do not wish the proceedings to be postponed. I wish to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add, I do have an assistant who can help me in part, and perhaps we can continue in this situation. I would prefer that to an interruption of the proceedings. So I am willing to waive the legal assistance so that the proceedings can continue and be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that even that requires a special procedure because the system here is that the right of a lawyer of your own choosing, of your own choice, exists under the Rules of this Tribunal. However, as in -- as is the case with special courts in several countries, before a lawyer can be admitted to plead before that particular court, authorisation must be sought and granted. And we have standards that need to be met by any lawyer, even if it's a lawyer of your own choosing that you are prepared to pay from your own pocket. So that is the Rule, and although I personally am very pleased to see your daughter sitting next to you, and I have had opportunity having her here in the courtroom in the Brdjanin case for months and months, still I am not the one to decide. It's the Registrar in accordance with the Rules. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So let's go back to this. Are you aware or have you come across the request made by Mrs. Maglov last week, I understand by email, for legal aid? MR. VAN de VLIET: Your Honour, as far as I understand, we have not received any request for legal aid. We have received a request to have her daughter assigned as a legal assistant, which was disconnected from that request that has now been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is the position with regard to Mrs. Jevtovic? MR. VAN de VLIET: We have rejected that request on the basis of internal policies and a rule that is in the directive which basically states that members of family of an accused, suspect, or counsel are not eligible for assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But wouldn't -- would not eligible for assignment under the legal aid system I would imagine? Because if you have your own brother or sister or father or mother or relative who is prepared to defend you pro bono without involving the resources of the Tribunal, then provided the other standards set by the Rules are met, I don't see how the family relationship or blood relationship has any importance. MR. VAN de VLIET: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have always been taught from even my university days, if you have a case of your own, never try to get a member of your family to defend you or never try to defend yourself because you tend to get too keyed up and too excited. But anyway, I do want feedback on both things. First of all, what is the procedure if Mrs. Maglov wants to proceed with her request for proper, full legal aid? MR. VAN de VLIET: If she wants to request for proper legal aid, she should submit her declaration of means, and that will be checked by the registry. If she is indeed found to be indigent, a counsel will be assigned to her on a temporary basis until the check has been completed and then can become a full-term basis or it can be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If she can provide you with sufficient information on her means today, is the registry or your office in a position to grant her request today? MR. VAN de VLIET: We would need more time to do the check. We could assign her a temporary counsel. We can try and find somebody on a short-term basis. We will try even today, but I cannot guarantee it. I can do my best. Excuse me, sorry. We have a list, a Rule 45 list, which contains a number of counsels who are readily available. So perhaps today or tomorrow we could find somebody. That's what I could guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with regard to her daughter? Is that -- the decision taken by your office is definitive, or are you prepared to reconsider it on the basis of what I mentioned regarding the relevance or otherwise of her relationship, mother/daughter relationship, considering that she is being sought as an assistant pro bono and not to be paid from the resources of this Tribunal. MR. VAN de VLIET: Yeah, I believe, definitely there's a difference between the case where Ms. Maglov is requesting for legal aid scheme to be applied or not. We will apply the Rule as it stands if she applies for legal aid. If she does not, there can definitely be more flexibility, although still the qualifications of somebody to be assigned as a legal assistant will be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But she was a legal assistant already in the Brdjanin case. Yes, perhaps, you can check on that. Mrs. Jevtovic, in the Brdjanin case, you had decided to leave yourself, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There was a money issue that you're well aware of. The Registrar at the time brought me under certain conditions at the time when I arrived, and they decided that they were not able to pay that amount any longer. And in the end, we found the compromise. I found the compromise with Mr. Ackerman, and the whole Defence team who was willing to keep me and support me in regard to the expenses that the Registrar would not cover any longer. However, during the break, due to my health situation, I couldn't travel, and I spent some four months in the hospital. That's the only reason I never came back for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I wanted just to make sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I have just one more information for you. In April, I passed my bar exam, so I am now a qualified lawyer under the rules of the country in which I reside, and would also like to add that all this was written and the email was sent to the Registrar, and we offered to submit them all the necessary paperwork and documentation for my appointment. But to date, we haven't received any reply. And I have the information on my computer that on 10th February, Ms. Maglov applied for the officially appointed legal counsel actually, and with the attached application for the appointment of the counsel. And I'm just surprised that they haven't received it. I have a copy of that, so we have it ready immediately today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. VAN de VLIET: Can I just clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. VAN de VLIET: We have received, as I understand, the application for Ms. Maglov's daughter, Ms. Jevtovic, to be assigned as a legal assistant. We have, as far as I understand, not received the request for legal aid to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So what I suggest be done is the following: Mrs. Maglov, if I understood her well, and please, if I did not, correct me, would not like today's sitting and the proceedings for that matter to be postponed pending the Registrar's decision on whether to assign counsel to her under the legal aid regime that we have. That's my understanding of what you said, Ms. Maglov. And that your preference would be to go ahead, particularly if your daughter is sitting by your side to assist you. Now, there are two options. One is a formal authorisation from the Registrar vis-a-vis Ms. Jevtovic, authorising her to assist Ms. Maglov in these proceedings with the understanding that this would not entail any remuneration from our part, from the part of the proceedings. But again, the decision is absolutely -- I would never even dream of interfering with the rights of the Registrar. This is his domain, and I will just not interfere with that. Please do keep in mind what was said here, and particularly also the fact that it appears -- not appears, I can confirm to you that Ms. Jevtovic was indeed one of the assistants in the Brdjanin trial. Were you a case manager, or what were you exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to Brdjanin case in 1999. In August 1999, I was assigned as interpreter. After that, I was assigned as the investigator. At the time when I arrived to assist Mr. Ackerman in the courtroom in The Hague, I was assigned as a legal assistant. And then when the issue of money arose, I have to say that then I was told that I was a case manager. I never got an assignment saying that I was a case manager. Only at that time they started referring to me as a case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't know whether you have authority to decide this yourself, or whether you have to refer it to Mr. Pimentel or even further up. How much time would you require to come back to us to confirm whether Ms. Jevtovic can act as legal assistant to her mother? That's number one. Number two, if that takes time, can I have - this is another alternative that I am asking you to look into - can I have the go-ahead from the Registrar to at least allow Ms. Jevtovic to sit next to her mother and be her assistant unofficially? Not as counsel, in other words. I mean, it's just unofficial. The position, as we usually follow it here, is that in the courtroom you're either a counsel or you're not. We do have legal assistants present, too, but normally it has only when they have been appointed by the Registrar. Otherwise, no one is allowed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to sit in here except maybe interns sometimes who are assisting either the Prosecution or the Defence. So I would like to have some kind of a clearance from your Office on this so we can go ahead and start. MR. VAN de VLIET: Your Honour, I understand that you have mentioned one possibility for the accused to follow, which is to waive the right to legal assistance but have her daughter assist her as a legal assistant. The other option, I think, was to apply for legal aid in full. In that case, we will have to follow the usual procedure, and we will come up with a counsel from the Rule 45 list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me correct you. As I understood it, Mrs. Maglov was prepared to waive her request for legal aid only -- only if the other request to have her daughter assigned as legal assistant was approved. If that's not the case, Mrs. Maglov, as I understood her, would prefer today's sitting to go ahead, to proceed, but she would not be waiving her right to ask for a Defence counsel. And that will be processed in due course, in its time. We are not going to finish the case today. It is very obvious. And she will then have counsel assigned to her if she is entitled to that, and he or she, that person will come on stage at the appropriate moment. That's how I understood you. And I see Ms. Maglov and Ms. Jevtovic nodding, which means at least I am not wrong. So that's a good thing to know. Yes. MR. VAN de VLIET: If you could give us a half hour to check the qualifications, as we have apparently received them already, then I think it would be fine to go ahead with Ms. Jevtovic as legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will suspend the sitting for half an hour, so that in the meantime try to do your homework and come back to us, please, with the confirmation. Yes, Ms. Maglov, please try to be as brief as you can so that we waste as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. May we please have a break of an hour and start at 11.00 because of some technical problems we are having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Technical problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small baby which the mother has to go and feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. All right. So can you live with that, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Most certainly, Your Honour. I wouldn't want to be accused of making a small baby hungry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have an idea what it means. I had forgotten what it was like with my daughters, but I have a grandson now. So I have come to terms with that. So it's okay. And a break of an hour. It will give you ample time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish to prolong this. But I would like to raise one additional issue I believe has been raised by Ms. Maglov's comments to you. In addition to the issues about legal assistance of her daughter and legal aid, she has also raised the issue of translation. I believe before we proceed, Ms. Maglov should indicate clearly to the Court that despite those problems, she is prepared to proceed in a knowing manner, or else I fear we may be proceeding with a person who is not yet ready to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I am not prepared to proceed with the case if the Rules have not been observed, and her rights have not been observed. So that I was coming to in due course. I would imagine that if her daughter is authorised to be present, then the fact that she is very fluent in English would help us surmount that problem. Am I reading you loud and clear, Ms. Maglov?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps you could take that in your baggage with you to the Registrar's office, and point that out to him, that it will save us having to postpone the sitting or adjourn outright.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever you said, Ms. Maglov, I understood you to say: "Yes, you are correct, Your Honour" that did not show up in the transcript. In other words, if your daughter is authorised to sit next to you and assist you, the fact that you have not received several documents in your language as yet, would you be prepared to ignore that for the time being so that we can proceed today, or would you still insist on having them translated in your own language before we can proceed with the testimony, with the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can proceed, but I am expecting the translations as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we'll have an hour's break, until 11.00. And hope the situation would have cleared up in the meantime. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So. Yes, good morning once more. Can I have a report on whether there is a decision by the Registrar's office on representation for Ms. Maglov. MR. VAN de VLIET: Yes, certainly. We have understood that Ms. Maglov will submit her declaration of means in the course of the day, thereby applying for legal aid. In the meantime, we have checked the qualifications of Ms. Jevtovic, and we have had her sign an undertaking that she will abide by the Rules and the code of conduct for counsel which would open up the road ahead for her to be a legal assistant to Ms. Maglov for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, do I take it that the situation as it is now, there is no objection on the part of the Registrar that Ms. Jevtovic acts as legal assistant in these proceedings pro bono? MR. VAN de VLIET: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct, okay. Ms. Maglov, on that basis, can we proceed with the evidence and with whatever needs to be done in this case even though the translations of some of -- of various documents in your own language have not been forwarded to you? I take it from the information that I have received that the pre-trial brief has been translated, and I think I have been told it will be handed over to you today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is -- there are the accompanying documents or some other documents that are being attended to. They are being translated, and it is hoped that the translation will be finished by the end of business today, and that means that basically you should have them available either later on today or early tomorrow morning. You have a right to ask this Trial Chamber to stay the proceedings until this is done, or you have also the right to waive that right and enable us, put us in a position which we can proceed. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. Although I have not received these translations, we may proceed. However, I have a question related to the preparation of the Defence. When am I supposed to submit my witness list and list of exhibits so that we could have enough time? That is to say, when the Prosecution completes its case, we should have enough time to call Defence witnesses, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let me make things clear. I don't want either of you, either Ms. Hollis, or you, Ms. Maglov, to form the idea that these proceedings will be as formal or as cumbersome as the proceedings in any normal trial that we have here. I intend to have these proceedings as simplified as possible, possibly -- I mean, this kind of case in my country would have lasted two hours, and it would be over. In other words, you would have been prepared -- would have come here prepared with all your witnesses, and you would have come here prepared with your witnesses. Today we would have heard them all and either have final Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. submissions immediately after, or postpone maybe for that purpose. If something comes up in the evidence that would prompt you to ask for some further witness, that might be considered. But that's about it. I mean, at the end of the day, you would get most of the time an oral decision, and that would be it. Here, it may be a little bit more cumbersome. But I do not intend to make it more cumbersome than it can be. So my idea was to start and possibly finish. So you have an intention of summoning witnesses, give us the list. The understanding is that if you need to update that list later on, you will be granted that right. But there is a limit. The idea was to start and finish this week. That was my intention. And that was the understanding when we discussed it at the pre-trial stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I thought it would be much shorter as well and that we would have sufficient time. Actually, it is the Prosecution motion that sought a postponement until the 23rd that created the greatest confusion in my mind. I thought that indeed there would be a postponement until the 23rd of March. However, I think that if we provide a list today, if I provide a list of witnesses today, we can complete all of this by Friday at the latest. My witness list is not long, really. I have one single witness, Mr. Peric, that is, who worked on the Defence team with me. So he knows about this, and he is prepared to come and testify. There's no problem involved whatsoever. It is only for the Victims and Witnesses Unit to contact him in due time, and then he should come. I don't know how the Prosecution case will evolve. Mr. Trbojevic could be a potential witness, and Mr. Zivko Bojic, that is to say, people who were on the Brdjanin Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: (redacted). That would be the witness list. And perhaps two exhibits, and that would be about it. That is what I would like to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed on this part, because you have mentioned several persons, do you have an interest in redacting the name of any one of them? Or is it okay with you if their names remain public? It's up to you. I mean, if you will be speaking some protective measures for any of them, then we will have the names redacted now while we are still in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I don't know is what the secretary's feelings are. I did not talk to her about this yet. She is supposed to testify only about one single detail, so there was no need to go through any kind of investigation with her. As for the other names I mentioned, there is no need for them not to testify in public, and we do not seek any protective measures for any one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to be on the safe side, I would rather prefer to be that, let's redact the secretary's name. And actually, the entire first two sentences of that paragraph. Can you follow me, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, page 16, lines 25 and 17, line 1. All right? Okay. I think that makes it safer. Yes, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. When studying the Rules, it was my understanding that I, as the accused party, can state my views, or rather enter a plea before -- before any witness is called and before any exhibit is produced. If so, I would wish to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. So let's start -- can we go ahead? I think Mr. Van de Vliet and Madam, you are excused. You can go back to your office. I thank you so much. You have been most helpful, and your contribution has been such that we can now proceed. I thank you so much. MR. VAN de VLIET: Most welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's agree on what procedure to follow. There has been a decision by this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, and then of course I'm open to any suggestions that you might have, was as follows: We have handed down a decision last week or whenever it was granting a motion which Ms. Hollis had filed for some amendments to be made to the indictment. Let's call it indictment. That, in turn, generates rights which you as an accused person, Ms. Maglov, have under our Rules. Our decision introduces actually new charges, and since you were co-counsel here, you also know what the rights are. And it also imposes on me as the Presiding Judge the obligation to ask you whether you want to enter a plea on the indictment as amended, or whether you want an adjournment to enable you to enter a plea because we do have new charges being introduced in the indictment. That's a right which you have under the Rules, and it's up to you to decide. So I think that's where we need to start from. Following that, if there is no objection on your part that we proceed today, and of course depending on your plea, then what I was -- what I would suggest is for Ms. Hollis to introduce the case in a very short introduction. I intended to ask you how much time you had in mind so I see whether I need to cut down on it, and we can then proceed with your witnesses. Is that -- do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Ms. Maglov, if you want to make a statement, of course, before we start with all this, you have every right to make it as well. All right? So let's proceed with the first -- with the first part. The indictment has been changed as a result, as a consequence of our decision. Do you want us to read the indictment as it now reads in its entirety, or do you waive that right? Let's start with this point first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to have the indictment read out to me because indeed I have never received it in my own language, so let me hear it now at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? You have never received the indictment -- the amended indictment in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I never saw this indictment, or perhaps I don't understand what the indictment is. If the indictment is that decision of the Chamber where there were only two paragraphs, then I did receive that. However, when referring to an indictment, I mean an indictment involving factual allegations as well. I never saw any such material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The factual allegations remained as they were. We did not change those. We only amended the indictment to read so as to include the attempt to intimidate or otherwise interfere with the witness, also the introduction of disclosure of the -- not just the identity, but also the whereabouts of the witness. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Basically I can -- we can do it this way. We had originally instructed the amicus curiae to lay out the charges against you in a formal document charging you with having intimidated -- intimidated the witness that we had mentioned earlier. And secondly, with having disclosed the identity of the witness to a member of the public in violation of an order pursuant to Rule 77(A)(ii), and that's the contempt Rule. Ms. Hollis asked for -- to have added in that charge "intimidating or otherwise interfering with" the witness. And we agreed to that. So the first charge levelled against you, Ms. Maglov, pursuant to Rule 77(A)(iv) is for having allegedly intimidated or otherwise interfered with the witness whose identity you are aware of. Then always pursuant to the motion that Ms. Hollis filed, we also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. granted the introduction in the indictment of a completely new charge; namely, attempting to intimidate or otherwise interfere with the witness, the identity of whom you are aware of. And this is -- would be pursuant to Rule 77(B). Then the original indictment had charged you with having disclosed the identity of the witness to a member of the public in violation of an order of this Chamber and pursuant to Rule 77(A)(ii). Upon the request of Ms. Hollis, we agreed to amend that, and now the charge does not only refer to disclosing the identity, but includes also disclosing the whereabouts, and the charge now reads: "Disclosing the identity and/or the whereabouts of the witness," whose identity you are aware of to a member of the public in violation of the same order to which the charges -- original charges referred to and pursuant to the same Rule, that is Rule 77(A)(ii). utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court, the Prosecution evidence in this case, both documentary and testimonial, will prove the following: At all times relevant to the allegations --

utterances.text: Yes -- 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At all times relevant to the allegations in this case, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's going to make it 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Witness, the alleged victim, lived and worked in an environment which was hostile toward persons seen to be acting contrary to the interests of Bosnian Serbs in general, and in particular hostile toward those persons who would testify before this Tribunal against a Serbian accused. The evidence will prove that witness was also in a vulnerable psychological and physical position because of his victimisation by Serb perpetrators during the armed conflict in Bosnia and because of his status as a non-Serb returnee to his home area. Witness was a member of the minority group in that area, both in terms of population numbers and in terms of those in power, including government officials, police, and business leaders. This is the context in which this Trial Chamber must evaluate the conduct of this respondent, conduct which gave rise to the allegations against her in these proceedings. The evidence will prove the following conduct of the respondent: Testimonial evidence and respondent's statements of 6 June 2002 will prove that during the time period between 1 September 2001 and 28 February 2002, respondent and a colleague had at least one personal contact with Witness, and that contact was in his office in a public, municipal building, surrounded by offices occupied by officials of Serb ethnicity. The evidence will prove that this contact was made after being advised by Witness R77-A, that Witness was a non-Serb returnee without previously informing Witness of respondent's role as a member of the Brdjanin Defence team and without obtaining Witness's prior informed consent to meet with her in that role. During the meeting, respondent never inquired whether Witness consented to meet with her at his office or elsewhere. Respondent did not immediately identify her role as a member of accused Brdjanin's Defence team, nor identify the purpose of the meeting, leaving Witness to initially conclude she was there to discuss redevelopment efforts in that geographic area. During the meeting, respondent and/or her colleague made argumentative statements to the witness, and respondent made the witness aware that she knew he had given a statement to the Tribunal and that he would be a witness in proceedings at the Tribunal. Given the situation, this "no notice meeting" with Witness in Witness's office created a coercive or threatening environment. Given the environment and the circumstances of the meeting, Witness was frightened for his safety and believed that respondent and her colleague meant either to threaten him or to try to influence his statement. Testimonial evidence and spontaneous's 6 June 2002 statement will also prove on the same occasion as the meeting with Witness or on a second occasion, respondent and her colleague met with witness R77-B in the same geographic area. Prior to this meeting, respondent had received and read Witness's unredacted Prosecution statement and knew that Witness was to be a Prosecution witness in the Brdjanin case. At the time of this meeting with Witness R77-B, the orders issued by the Brdjanin Pre-Trial Chamber in its decision on motion by Prosecution for protective measures had been in effect for over one year. Those orders included prohibiting the Brdjanin Defence from disclosing to the public the names, identifying information, or whereabouts of any witness or potential witness identified to them by the Prosecutor, unless such disclosure was directly and specifically necessary for the preparation and presentation of the Brdjanin case. As defined in the order, the Brdjanin Defence included this respondent. Nonetheless, in the presence of Witness R77-B, respondent disclosed that Witness had given a statement to the Prosecution and that Witness was to be a witness in proceedings before this Tribunal. The evidence will prove that the respondent's conduct was willful, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that is, deliberate, and that respondent, an experienced attorney who had performed a legal role in the Brdjanin Defence team beginning in August 1999, engaged in the conduct knowingly. Regarding the allegation of intimidation or other interference with Witness or the attempt to do so, respondent had several sources of information regarding the existence of the hostile environment in which the alleged victim lived and worked. First, her personal association with the relevant geographic area. Secondly, respondent had resort to Prosecution pleadings and documentary submissions to include, firstly, the Prosecution motion for protective measures filed on 10 January 2000 and served on lead Defence counsel on this same date. This pleading put the Defence on notice of the alleged risk to potential witnesses in Bosnia and the generalised fears of potential Prosecution witnesses regarding their safety and security. Secondly, the confidential Appendix B to the Prosecution's second motion for protective measures for victims and witnesses filed on 31 July 2000 and served on lead Defence counsel on the same date. This document, a security assessment, concluded that non-Serbs living in the geographic area in question were at considerable risk if they testified against a Serb. Respondent also had as a source of knowledge the 3 July 2000 Pre-Trial Chamber decision mentioned previously. This decision recognised the vulnerability of Prosecution witnesses and potential witnesses when it prohibited the Defence team from disclosing confidential or nonpublic Prosecution materials to the media and from disclosing to the public identifying information regarding Prosecution witnesses or potential witnesses. Both documentary and testimonial evidence will also prove that during the relevant time period, the respondent had knowledge or access to knowledge of the vulnerable status of the Witness, including that he was a potential target of the hostile environment in which he worked and lived. One source of this knowledge was Prosecution disclosure that was received by the lead Defence counsel on 14 May 2001. This disclosure included the unredacted Prosecution statement of Witness in which he detailed his mistreatment during the conflict. Respondent confirmed in her 6 June 2002 statement that at least by December 2001, she had received and read this statement. Another source of knowledge was a 2 November 2001 Prosecution filing served on lead Defence counsel on 5 November. In this filing, the Prosecution listed its witnesses for the geographic area relevant to this proceeding, including Witness, as one of those who would testify. This filing provided respondent further knowledge or access to knowledge that Witness would be called to testify, and thus was a vulnerable target of the hostile environment in which he lived and worked. In addition, as mentioned previously, respondent had this knowledge from Witness R77-A who informed respondent of Witness's name, ethnicity, and status as a returnee to the area prior to respondent having personal contact with Witness. Armed with this information or access to it, respondent nonetheless carried out the "no notice" meeting with Witness in a coercive setting. In regard to the allegation that respondent violated an order of the Chamber, respondent had knowledge or access to knowledge of the 3 July order for nondisclosure to the public of Witness's identity and whereabouts, this decision and this order, as mentioned earlier, having been served on lead Defence counsel on 3 July 2000. As mentioned previously, respondent confirmed that she had received and read Witness's statement and knew Witness was a witness before disclosing the information to Witness R77-B. Another source which gave respondent notice of the existence of this order was the receipt for disclosure material which was signed for by lead Defence counsel on 14 May 2001. In its receipt, the Prosecution reminds lead Defence counsel that the materials are provided on the basis that they will be dealt with in accordance with the rulings given by the Trial Chamber in its decision dated 3 July 2000. The documentary and testimonial evidence in this case will prove that this respondent engaged in misconduct deliberately and with the requisite knowledge, and that her conduct constituted the contempt of the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV

Yes. If you wish to state anything else, Ms. Maglov, you have a right to do so just as you have a right to remain silent. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to add something, Your Honour. At the time when for the first time in my life I saw that witness, we will not mention his name, so I will continue to use the term "Witness," we interviewed the witness with the intention to see whether he would agree to be a Defence witness. That was our intention to begin with. As I explained in detail, I won't go into it any further. But I also wish to say that the atmosphere at that time was very friendly. We talked in a pleasant atmosphere. I wish to stress that we did introduce ourselves at the beginning, that we were announced by the secretary, so we did not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. enter the room where the witness was unannounced. And before starting any kind of interview with the witness, we introduced ourselves as members of Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team. We exchanged visiting cards. And I still have the visiting card in my possession. I will later tender it into evidence. I deeply, deeply regret, because I know the suffering that people went through in that area, including this witness, I am really sorry if my visit contributed to increasing his suffering. Later on, when I read all his statements, it is certainly true that reminding the witness to the things that he suffered is certainly very difficult for him and awakens very bad memories. So I'm certain that afterwards the witness did think about this and that he did feel upset. However, it is my submission that my behaviour and the behaviour of my colleague did not give rise to any response in the witness right away that would make us feel that the witness did not wish to talk to us. The witness spoke to us to the extent that he wished to do so. The interview did not last long. I can't remember exactly, but I think it was not more than 40 minutes at the most. And we parted in a friendly atmosphere. We said good-bye, and so we parted. From the evidence we shall tender, it will be clear that we really did not know at the time that this was a Prosecution witness. The entire interview with this witness was, and of course when you approach a witness for the first time, a potential witness, you will of course act in a way that will not alienate the witness and make him say he doesn't want to give an interview. And for this reason, I introduced myself rather more extensively than I normally would. I think I have clarified this point. As for disclosure, I really never, never had an opportunity to see or know about the Trial Chamber's decision on protective measures. I had no idea that protective measures were in existence. I would never have deliberately contravened any order by this Trial Chamber precisely because I am an attorney-at-law with many years of experience. Furthermore, in my country, the practice and the rules when talking to witnesses are quite different than they are here. In my country, all witnesses are court witnesses. There is no strict division between who was bringing in the witness. It doesn't matter who brought the witness in. That's how I am used to working. That's how I worked for 30 years. I never had to focus on whose witness somebody was; everybody was a court witness. It was in our interest for a witness who had something to say to come before the Court and tell the truth because the truth is the only possible defence. I did not disclose either the witness's name or his whereabouts. It was due to a combination of circumstances - I don't go into details now - that the second time we met the witness, this was in the corridor, and the secretary who was there, because Witness 77-B and I had arrived to look for Mr. Peric who was supposed to be in the mayor's office, but the mayor wasn't there. And the secretary told us where Mr. Peric was. And in this interval of time, between our talk -- our conversation with the secretary and the time we needed to reach the witness's office, we could have spoken for two or three minutes at the most. I can't remember how long it was exactly. And the witness, that is, Witness 77-B, said that he knew the witness very well and why shouldn't we drop in, because they were good friends. They had worked together in the school. And that's why at that point in time, I entered the witness's office. On the second visit, I knew that there was a statement. I didn't know whether he would actually be in a witness because the statement we had in our file dated back to 1996 or 1997, I think, and it was quite clearly stated on that statement that the witness was to testify in public. Regardless of this, I did not disclose either the witness's name or his whereabouts, or rather his workplace. I did not disclose this because first of all I didn't even know that he was a protected witness. I was not aware that if I received this statement, that this witness could be protected. When we as the Defence team conducted our work, we never talked to any Prosecution witnesses. This was the first one, and it was quite by chance because somebody else had told us about him. It was Witness 77-A who said, well, there are returnees here. You might want to talk to so-and-so. And we accepted this suggestion. And we learned all the rest later on. So not for a minute did we intend to do anything to obstruct the work of the Tribunal. On the contrary, our position was that people should come and testify, especially people who had something to say, to assist the Tribunal in arriving at the truth. I am very sorry, and I deeply regret that this witness suffered what he did. At the time, I didn't know about all his sufferings. I'm sure that our visit contributed to increasing his suffering in some way but reminding him of what he'd been through. For this reason, I intend to call the secretary as a witness to testify to these circumstances. Furthermore, I wish to mention briefly something that the Prosecutor said here, and that is that Witness 77-A is not a Serb. I think this should be corrected because the witness actually is a Serb. Furthermore, the Prosecutor said that the witness endured suffering because of the Serbs. I'm not sure whether she is referring to the period in which the witness made a statement or was a potential witness, or whether she was referring to the sufferings of 1992, during the war. These are two very different things. In my view, regardless of the whole combination of circumstances in which all this took place, I think the witness never experienced any unpleasantness because of our visit which I believe did upset him. I can say that now. And that's all I have to say at present.

utterances.text: All right. Madam Chuqing, since it contains the name and other information with regard of the witness, the list being tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, in accordance with a previous ruling in this matter, any matters which were filed confidentially remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P7 and P7.1, Your Honours, are the statements of Witness, the unredacted OTP statements of Witness, which were disclosed in the material provided to Mr. Ackerman for which he signed on 14 May 2001. I am providing both the English copy, which is Exhibit P7, and the B/C/S copy, which is Exhibit 7.1. Both the B/C/S and the English were disclosed on that date. That would also be a confidential exhibit. Exhibit P8 is a confidential Prosecution list of witnesses and exhibits filed pursuant to Rules of Procedure and Evidence 65 ter (ii) and (iii). I have redacted that to show only Witness as a witness in the relevant geographic area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And also included in that exhibit is the Registry distribution sheet showing distribution of this 2 November filing to lead Defence counsel on 5 November 2001. Exhibit P9 is a confidential, under-seal addendum to the Prosecution's 11th motion for protective measures for victims and witnesses. The addendum filed on 12 September 2002, and the Registry distribution sheet showing service on lead Defence counsel on 12 September 2002. This filing, of course, is outside the relevant time period for this matter. The purpose of the filing is to show that the hostile environment continued to exist throughout the time period in question in these proceedings. Your Honours, Exhibit P10 and 10.1 are the statement of the respondent taken by the amicus curiae investigator signed by the respondent on 6 September 2002. P10 is the English version of that statement, and P10.1 is the B/C/S version of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Insofar as I'm just speaking from my memory -- insofar as this statement might refer to the witness by his name, that's the case, then this statement will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't believe it does. But caution is the better part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, even if it doesn't, it's still very indicative of who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And statements typically are nonpublic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, Exhibit P11 and 11.1 is the verbatim record of interview of Ms. Maglov conducted by the amicus curiae investigator. It is this interview which forms the basis for Exhibit P10 and 10.1, the signed statement. I introduce this because the record of interview and the statements are not word for word, and this is something the Chamber may wish to explore in determining the credibility of these exhibits. And I have both the record of interview in English and the record of interview in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we come to P12, which has not yet been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. P12 is a chart, an Excel sheet, Microsoft Excel sheet showing the respondent's travel periods to the Tribunal, including during the relevant time periods. When I was here in December, I had requested of the Registry if they had records to indicate any periods of presence in the Tribunal. They had not been able to find any such records. I renewed that request after the deadline for disclosure. At that time, they sent me this sheet. I did email it to the respondent as soon as I received it. When I arrived here on the 12th, I called OLAD and asked them if they had provided an explanatory cover sheet for this Excel sheet as I had requested. They indicated the Registrar had provided such a cover sheet. They also indicated that they had amended the chart to add a column to show an authorisation number for the travel. I have not had the opportunity to provide the amended copy of this sheet to Ms. Maglov, nor have I had the opportunity to provide her with the Registrar's cover sheet. The purpose of the cover sheet was to show that it did originate in the Registry and was an accurate record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And with that, I think we can have a break. In the meantime, Ms. Maglov, if you want to raise any objection to the admissibility of any of these documents, you will do that any of these documents, do you live that --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. You will raise that at the beginning of the sitting immediately after the break. Thank you. There will be a break of 25 minutes. Thank you. Let's have the document, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While they're distributing the document, Your Honour, as one last matter, I would ask this Chamber to judicially notice the practice of this Tribunal to serve pleadings and other filings and decisions on lead counsel for each side for distribution to the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your request has been put on record, and we will decide on that. I don't think there can be any other way of approaching that problem. It would be the antithesis --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's ridiculing the whole system were it different. We will have a look at this last document. All right. We'll have a break of 25 minutes, and we'll deal with the rest as we go along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so Ms. Maglov, is there any objection or is there an objection to the admissibility of any one of these 12 documents, to start with?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the tendered documents, I see that the documents tendered are mostly decisions on protective measures which the lead counsel received. I do not see a single piece of evidence here which would show how, when, and in what manner I could have been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's a separate matter. That's a separate matter. That's a separate matter. That's a question of proof that may or may not arise, depending on how the case for the Prosecution and the case for the Defence go, in which direction they go. So the fact that they were not received -- they were received by Mr. Ackerman actually points out to the practice that Ms. Hollis referred to at the end of the -- at the end of the previous session; namely, whereby she asked us to judicially take notice of the practice of this Tribunal to serve pleadings and other filings and decisions on lead counsel for each side for distribution to the team. Essentially, it goes to the core of the whole -- I don't think there is a contention that none of these documents were actually served on you by the Trial Chamber -- sorry, by the Tribunal. I don't think you are contesting that, Ms. Hollis. So what you say really doesn't have any relevance at all as regards the admissibility of the documents because the documents, according to the practice of this Tribunal, are served on the lead counsel and not on any of the other members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously whether you were made aware of them is another matter, if it is relevant at all. Yes, apart from that, do you have any particular objection with any of these documents? I take it, and that is an undertaking, that if there are any of them which are not translated and need to be translated, then they will be translated. So that way I am obviating against any further objection on that basis. As far as these documents are concerned, apart from what I said, do you have any objection towards their admissibility at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P10, or rather, P10.1, I object to it. I object to its admission as an exhibit because the statement I made was made in good faith as a statement to the amicus curiae who was to judge from my statement -- I can't even call it a statement. It was an explanation I gave in order to convince the amicus that we were really doing nothing wrong. So I didn't even state that I remembered some details about the meeting, so it's not really a statement concerning the event; rather, it's my explanation to make the amicus understand our manner of working, how we thought, and how we in the Defence team discussed matters. Although it's my voice, when I listened to the tape I didn't understand it myself. If this is meant to be a statement, I should have been given an opportunity, because there are many things that are unclear, that are vague. When I'm explaining some things, it's not evident who I'm referring to without additional explanations, but this was not presented to me as a statement. And I was not given an opportunity to clarify it, and that's the reason I object to it. Because initially, I did not understand that this was an investigation. I thought the amicus curiae, a friend of the Court, was simply trying to ascertain certain facts. I didn't state that I remembered where we had been, what we talked about, and so on. I was simply trying to explain to the amicus what we did and how. Nothing else. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, do you have any remarks on the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In regards to Exhibit P10 and 10.1, that is the statement with respondent's signature on it. And it is at the beginning of the statement she indicates she has -- she understanding her rights and is willing to make a statement. I'm a little confused. Perhaps Ms. Maglov was also speaking to 11 and 11.1, which is the record of interview. But as to 10 and 10.1, I would suggest that her objection is more in the way of an explanation that might impact the weight of the document but not the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to clear this up, Ms. Maglov, are we talking of P10, or are we talking of P11? That's what she mentioned before. She referred to P10.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I'm referring to both. Both of these were simply my attempts to explain. I was not given an opportunity to clarify points that are not clear. I was not given an opportunity to clarify and clear up ambiguities. Therefore, this cannot be taken as a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And with regard to P11, Ms. Hollis, what's your response?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, P11 is based on the tape of the interview which was provided to me when I became amicus curiae prosecutor. Mr. Ukropina, who was the amicus curiae investigator, had prepared that tape and indicated that was the interview of Ms. Maglov. That was submitted to the Registry for translation, and so it is, according to the Registry, as near as possible a verbatim translation of the tape that they were provided. Again, I would suggest first of all that Ms. Maglov's objections are more in the way of an explanation that may go to the weight of the document rather than an objection to the authenticity of the document. Secondly, I have here in The Hague, the amicus curiae investigator whom I intend to call, to have him explain the procedures he went through in regard to both taking the interview and preparing the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me explain our position. We will for all intents of purposes of law constitute an oral decision that we are taking. We've taken into account your submissions, Ms. Maglov, and also your response, Ms. Hollis. We consider as important the following factors: Number one is particularly with regard to P10, this formed part of a -- the considerations which the previous amicus curiae took into account when formulating his report to the Trial Chamber on the basis of which then this Trial Chamber decided to institute proceedings or to proceed with proceedings for contempt against Ms. Maglov. So even from that point of view, the presence of the statement in the records becomes imperative. With regard to P11, the position that we take is that for the time being, this is considered to be of sufficient importance to be admitted with the caveat that we will, if necessary, revise our decision later on when the previous amicus curiae has testified on the -- particularly on the manner in which this interview was suggested in the first place and obtained and whether it served as a basis for his considerations, in which case then, of course, other considerations will come into place. So the final decision on this document, in particular, we will take later on. Okay. Can we proceed now with the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would call Witness R77-B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: R77-B. I think we need to pull down the curtains, first. While we are waiting for the witness to come forward, Ms. Maglov, I was going to suggest to you more from a practical point of view than as anything else to submit to the Registrar, Madam Chuqing, a list of the witnesses you intend to bring forward, even if you may be doubtful with regard to one or more of them. So that steps are taken straight away by the office, the relevant office, to ensure their attendance. If we can do that this week, I think it will spare you unnecessary expense of having to come back. I think it will be wise to follow my advice, but it's up to you. This is without prejudice. In other words, if you want to call more witnesses eventually, you'll have all the opportunity. If you want to renounce any of these witnesses, you will have a right to do that, of course, without prejudice. But I would suggest that you hand in the details to the Registrar so we can start working on it because time flies. Yes, usher, would you bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is facial and voice distortion, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon actually. It's good afternoon now. Time flies, as I just said a few minutes ago. And welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned by the Prosecution in this case to give evidence in contempt proceedings that have been instituted against Ms. Maglov, Milka Maglov. And before you proceed with your testimony, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the gentleman standing at your right is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair. And let me explain to you briefly what's going to happen. First of all, I welcome you once more. You have been summoned as a witness for the Prosecution. The Prosecution on your behalf has asked for certain protective measures. I'm going to explain them to you very briefly. The first one is that your name will remain hidden. No one is going to refer to you by your name and surname. We will refer to you by means of a number. And for your information, you are Witness 77-B. Witness 77-B. The second is that although you'll be testifying in open session, no one will be able to see your face. We have mounted a facial distortion apparatus, and the moment the cameras are focussed on you, you will see a lot of squares, and that's how others will see you. No one will be able to see your face on the monitor from wherever they might be receiving. This is precisely how you will appear to outsiders. The third protective measures that we have undertaken to protect -- to hide your identity by way of protecting you is to put in place a voice distortion. In other words, no one will be able to hear your real voice. Members of the public who will be outside this courtroom following these proceedings will hear a different voice, voice of someone else. It will be your voice, but it is distorted. Are you satisfied with these protective measures?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, the witness's microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our people say whatever is necessary is not hard to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slight technical problem in the French booth. Just a moment, please. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, one moment please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I could tell you exactly what the witness said, and then you can interpret it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Do you need to translate the witness's statement, or I suppose you have it on your screen, at line -- yes, page 14 -- page 50, line 14 and 15. I'm addressing the interpreters in the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're working on the sound, Your Honour. Sorry, there's a slight technical problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you are ready to proceed, please tell us, and we will go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, we also took the precaution of pulling down the curtains that you hear now going up so that no member of the public who could be maybe sitting in the gallery could see you as you walked in the courtroom. That's another measure we put in place to protect, hide your identity. Is the problem in the French booth sorted out?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And so let's proceed. You are going to be first handed a small sheet of your paper with your name and surname on it. Have a look at it, and then just tell us whether that is your real name and surname, just say yes, correct, or no, not correct. But don't read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please show it to Ms. Maglov. All right. Let's have a look at it ourselves. Yes, you are first going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Hollis, who is representing the Prosecution in this case as per instructions of this Trial Chamber and a decision of the Registrar. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, Your Honour, the sheet which was shown to the witness was marked Exhibit P13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will go under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Hollis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Sir, the sheet that you were shown, does that sheet also reflect your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to about the 19th of December 2001 and ask you on that date do you recall meeting with the respondent, Ms. Milka Maglov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, prior to this meeting, had you heard of Milka Maglov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: Before this meeting, of course I had heard of Ms. Maglov because I am good friends with her brother, and I also knew and still know her daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time of this meeting, were you aware of her profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: I knew that she was an attorney prior to the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the meeting on or about the 19th of December, where did you initially meet with respondent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: The meeting was agreed on by telephone. Up to 1995, I lived in Bosnia. Then I moved to Vojvodina in Serbia. And I had problems with the restoration of my tenancy rights in my flat in Bosnia. After I was handed the decision on the restoration of my tenancy rights, my former secondary school where I used to work, through the public attorney's office of Republika Srpska instituted proceedings to have my tenancy rights taken away from me. I then asked Ms. Maglov's brother to give me her telephone number as she was an attorney and I wanted her to represent me at the session at the court in Kotor Varos. Of course, I intended to be present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you initially began your meeting with Ms. Maglov, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: The meeting was agreed on -- it was agreed that we would meet in her brother's shop in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: This happened on the 19th of December 2001. I think it was at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, who if anyone was with Ms. Maglov on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: On that day, Mr. Peric arrived with Ms. Maglov by car from Banja Luka. He was an attorney who had lived in Tuzla before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you had this meeting with Mr. Peric and the respondent, Ms. Maglov, what, if anything, did they tell you regarding their role in the Brdjanin trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R77-B
utterances.text: They told me on that occasion that they were members of Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to go into private session because my questions will elicit information that could disclose the identity of this witness as well as Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
